q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which Britain's natural resources contributed to industrialization in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why industrialization began in Britain rather than in another region, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which industrialization changed systems of labor in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.

sample_answers.a: Britain held large, accessible coal deposits near navigable rivers and ports. Coal supplied cheap energy for steam engines and for smelting iron, while waterways moved coal, raw materials, and finished goods at low cost.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, Britain's high wages relative to cheap energy gave employers a direct profit motive to invest in labor-saving machinery. In regions where labor was cheap, mechanization offered little return, so the incentive to industrialize was weaker.
sample_answers.c: Industrialization moved production out of homes and small workshops into factories, where wage laborers worked long, regimented shifts under employer supervision instead of setting their own pace as artisans or cottage workers had.

q1.stimulus:
Historians have long debated why industrialization began in Britain rather than elsewhere in the world. One influential interpretation argues that Britain's advantages were not only technological but also institutional and ecological. Britain possessed abundant coal deposits situated near navigable waterways, a legal system that protected property and enforced contracts, and a culture of mechanical experimentation encouraged by scientific societies. Crucially, British wages were high relative to the cost of energy, which made it profitable for manufacturers to invest in labor-saving machinery; in regions where human labor was cheap, such investments offered little return. In this view, industrialization was less a sudden breakthrough than the result of specific economic incentives aligning with available resources.
—Historian's account of the Industrial Revolution in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Smith makes about the division of labor.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the division of labor increased manufacturing output during the Industrial Revolution.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of Smith's account as evidence about working conditions during the Industrial Revolution.

sample_answers.a: Smith claims that dividing pin-making into about eighteen distinct operations, each performed by a specialized worker, multiplies output enormously: a lone unspecialized worker could make at most twenty pins a day, while specialized workers together produce thousands.
sample_answers.b: When each worker repeated a single simple task, workers became faster through practice and no time was lost switching between different operations or tools, so the same number of workers produced far more goods.
sample_answers.c: Smith analyzes efficiency and output but says nothing about wages, hours, discipline, or safety. His account therefore cannot show whether the productivity gains came at the expense of the workers' health or well-being.

q2.stimulus:
To take an example from a very trifling manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has been very often taken notice of: the trade of the pin-maker. A workman not educated to this business, nor acquainted with the use of the machinery employed in it, could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But in the way in which this business is now carried on, not only the whole work is a peculiar trade, but it is divided into a number of branches. One man draws out the wire, another straights it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head; to make the head requires two or three distinct operations; to put it on is a peculiar business, to whiten the pins is another; it is even a trade by itself to put them into the paper; and the important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations.
—Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 1776

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the painting that connects it to the Industrial Revolution.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the technology shown in the painting changed iron production in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.c: Explain ONE environmental effect of the industrial processes depicted in the painting.

sample_answers.a: The painting shows coke-fired blast furnaces glowing at night, which indicates large-scale, coal-powered ironworks operating around the clock — the continuous, energy-intensive production characteristic of industrialization.
sample_answers.b: Smelting iron with coke (purified coal) instead of charcoal freed ironmakers from dependence on timber and allowed far larger furnaces; output rose from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tons, making iron cheap enough for machinery, railways, and bridges.
sample_answers.c: Coal-fired furnaces released heavy smoke and soot into the air, polluting nearby towns, while the demand for coal led to extensive mining that scarred the landscape and the burning of fossil fuels on an unprecedented scale.

q3.stimulus: The image is Philip James de Loutherbourg's 1801 oil painting Coalbrookdale by Night, depicting the Bedlam Furnaces of the Coalbrookdale Company in Shropshire, England. Coke-fired blast furnaces blaze against the night sky while workers, horses, and carts move among piles of coal and iron in the foreground. Coalbrookdale was among the first sites to smelt iron with coke, and the painting came to symbolize the birth of the Industrial Revolution.
